Timperley Writes
Volume On China
“What War Means—The Japanese Terror in China” by H. J. Timperley, China correspondent of the Manchester Guardian, is announced by the London publishing firm of Victor Gollancz Ltd. for issue early next month.
Advance notices say that “sordid details of the Japanese invasion of China and of its attendant brutalities have appeared with sickening regularity upon the front pages of the world’s newspapers. It may be questioned, however, whether it is generally realized that the reports of rape and loot and general bestiality flashed over the cables were based on signed eye-witness accounts obtained from unimpeachable sources. It is probable that no situation of the kind has been so fully documented from authentic neutral quarters....”
Mr. Timperley’s book is termed “a damning indictment of war in general and in particular of the terrorism employed by the Japanese Army in its hitherto unsuccessful effort to reduce the Chinese nation to a state of cowed submission. In this volume are gathered letters, case reports, and documents, the most pertinent of which have been supplied by absolutely neutral observers.... The object....is not to stir up animosity against the Japanese people, but to give the world an accurate picture of the Japanese army’s treatment of the Chinese civilian population....”
Mr. Timperley, a China resident since 1921, is now in Europe.

EDITORIAL SUMMARY
CREATES DISPUTE

British Consul-General
Informed Of Affair
By Journalist

With his censorship dispute with the Japanese authorities Monday still unsettled, Mr. H. J. Timperley, correspondent for the Manchester Guardian, yesterday had his second clash with the Nipponese censors when they held up another of his news messages.

Mr. Timperley's message, which he filed at the cable office at about 1.30 p.m., summarized an editorial appearing in yesterday's North-China Daily News, which dealt with the alleged conduct of the Japanese troops in Nanking.

At about 3.45 p.m. the Guardian correspondent received a telephonic message from a Japanese censor, asking him to withdraw the dispatch, asserting that the information contained in the message was only a newspaper report.

Phillips Informed

When Mr. Timperley explained that he had received independent confirmation from private sources to support the message he sent, the censor informed him that unless the dispatch were withdrawn, it would be stopped.

Immediately after the telephone conversation, the correspondent reported the matter to the British Consul-General, Mr. Herbert Phillips. In his communication with Mr. Phillips, the newsman contended that his message was "arbitrarily" and "unwarrantedly suppressed" by the Japanese authorities. He requested the British Consul-General to make representations to the Japanese in order that his reports to the Guardian would not be either suppressed or censored.

At the Japanese press conference yesterday afternoon, the Japanese Embassy spokesman announced that substantiated news reports maliciously tending to besmirch the good name of the Nipponese army will be suppressed hereafter regardless of source. He explained that Japanese were holding up dispatches filed by Mr. Timperley which were based on the North-China Daily News account of the alleged conditions in Nanking. He said that the alleged figures contained in the report were grossly exaggerated.

During the conference the question of mail censorship was raised by Mr. Hallet Abend, New York Times correspondent, who informed the Japanese spokesman that letters from his paper which arrived on the U.S.S. Pillsbury had been opened. The spokesman declared that no mail censorship was in progress here and promised an investigation.

Editorial Quoted

The disputed dispatch of Mr. Timperley, quoting the North-China Daily News editorial, stated that "to the astonishment of most people, raping, abduction of women and looting continued in Nanking until the last few days. It is estimated that more than 10,000 people had been killed," the dispatch continued. "How many women had been raped is impossible to ascertain, but estimates vary as low as 8,000 to as high as 20,000," the message said. 此事

周一与日本当局在审查问题上的争端仍未解决，《曼彻斯特·卫报》记者 H. J. 田伯烈先生昨天又与日本审查员发生第二次冲突，后者扣留了他的另一条新闻消息。

田伯烈先生于下午1点30分左右在电报局发出的消息，总结了昨日《字林西报》刊登的一篇社论，该社论涉及日军在南京的所谓行为。

下午3点45分左右，这位《卫报》记者接到一名日本审查员的电话，要求他撤回该电文，声称消息中包含的信息仅是一份报纸报道。

菲利普斯获悉

当田伯烈先生解释说他已从私人渠道获得独立证实以支持他发送的消息时，审查员告诉他，除非撤回电文，否则将被拦截。

通话结束后，记者立即向英国总领事赫伯特·菲利普斯（Herbert Phillips）先生报告了此事。在与菲利普斯先生的沟通中，这位新闻工作者声称他的消息被日本当局“任意”且“毫无理由地”压制。他请求英国总领事向日本方面提出交涉，以确保他发给《卫报》的报道不被压制或审查。

在昨天下午的日本新闻发布会上，日本大使馆发言人宣布，今后无论来源如何，都将压制那些有据可查但恶意损害日本军队名誉的新闻报道。他解释说，日本人正在扣留田伯烈先生提交的电文，这些电文基于《字林西报》关于南京所谓状况的报道。他说，报道中所谓的数字被严重夸大。

会议期间，《纽约时报》记者哈莱特·阿本德（Hallet Abend）先生提出了邮件审查的问题，他告知日本发言人，他的报社寄来并随美国海军“皮尔斯伯里号”（U.S.S. Pillsbury）抵达的信件已被拆封。发言人宣称此处并未进行邮件审查，并承诺进行调查。

引用社论

田伯烈先生引起争议的电文引用了《字林西报》的社论，称“令大多数人惊讶的是，强奸、绑架妇女和抢劫行为在南京一直持续到最近几天。据估计，已有超过10,000人被杀，”电文继续说道。“有多少妇女被强奸无法确定，但估计数字低至8,000，高达20,000，”消息中说。“年仅11岁的女孩和53岁的妇女都遭到侵犯，”发给《卫报》的报道说。

MR. H. J. TIMPERLY
EXPLAINS
Editor,
THE SHANGHAI TIMES
Sir,—As there appears to be some misconception with regard to the press despatch filed by myself to the Manchester "Guardian" which was suppressed by the Japanese authorities I should be glad if you would allow me to make clear the following points:
(1) The message was not merely delayed, as has been suggested in some newspaper reports, but was in fact, suppressed. So far as I am aware it has not yet been released for transmission.
(2) The report that my message contained statements to the effect that "300,000 Chinese civilians had been executed following the Japanese occupation of the Shanghai-Nanking area" is incorrect. What I did say was: "A survey by one competent foreign observer indicates that in the Yangtze delta no less than 300,000 Chinese civilians have been slaughtered—in many cases in cold blood."
(3) The action of the Japanese authorities in waiting for 14 hours before getting into touch with me about the matter and then asking me to proceed to the Japanese Military Headquarters was sufficiently highhanded, but does not constitute the main ground of my complaint. I contend that the Japanese have no right to interfere in any way with message lodged at the cable offices by British correspondents for transmission abroad. If they think they have cause for complaint against the correspondents their proper course of action surely is to take up the matter with the British authorities. If the Japanese are to be allowed to suppress telegrams which they don't like why should not the British and, for that matter, all of the other powers who are partners in the administration of the International Settlement claim an equal right? It must not be forgotten that, all appearances to the contrary, Japan has not formally declared war upon China. How long are we going to allow her to have her cake and eat it too?
H. J. TIMPERLY.
Shanghai, January 18, 1938.

Question Over Holding Up Of

In reply to a question at yester-

the Japanese Government, but as a
last resort the Army had the final
word.

Mr. Timperley did not raise the
question, which had been voiced by
another correspondent, but in reply
to an invitation to speak privately to
the Embassy spokesman, M. Okimura,
he stated that this was impossible
as he had already taken up the
matter officially with Embassy and
Consular officials. It then was stated

had approached Mr. Okimura, who
replied that he would speak with
Mr. Timperley regarding the censor-
ship. The latter put no further
remarks forward.

Replying to another question, the
spokesman stated that there had been
some misunderstanding about a report
that the correspondent in question
had been summoned to the Japanese
Military Headquarters—as Mr. Tim-
perley had reported—it was meant
as an invitation to discuss the tele-
gram with the military attaché. They
regretted the misunderstanding; what
was meant was to discuss it with a
competent military official.

Mr. Timperley then asked if the
message had been sent, the reply
being, "The message was to have
been sent if the correspondent and
the military had come to see the
matter eye to eye—in spite of his
efforts to get in touch with the
correspondent, the censor had not

关于扣留
记者消息的疑问

在昨天的日本新闻发布会上，针对为何《曼彻斯特·卫报》记者 H. J. 田伯烈先生于周日晚上提交的一条消息在审查过程中经历了15小时延误的问题，发言人表示，“自从日本军队占领上海以来，审查是日本军队的权利和特权。起初的审查由受雇于日本政府的平民进行，但最终决定权在于军队。

田伯烈先生没有提出这个问题，该问题是由另一位记者提出的，但在回应私下与大使馆发言人奥村（Okimura，音译）先生交谈的邀请时，他表示这是不可能的，因为他已经正式向大使馆和领事馆官员提出了此事。随后有人指出，陛下政府的领事官员已接触奥村先生，后者回答说他将与田伯烈先生谈谈审查事宜。后者未再发表进一步评论。

在回答另一个问题时，发言人表示，关于涉事记者被传唤至日本军事总部的报道存在一些误解——正如田伯烈先生所报告的那样——这原本是被邀请与武官讨论该电报。他们对这一误解表示遗憾；本意是与一位合格的军事官员进行讨论。

田伯烈先生随后询问该消息是否已发出，回答是，“如果记者和军方在该问题上达成一致，消息本应发出——尽管审查员努力联系记者，但未能做到。”田伯烈先生回答说，“我今天中午12点前一直在家。”

其他记者询问这是否意味着不存在公开审查，即新闻代表是否会被告知审查员是否拦截了消息。发言人回答说，日本的意图是维持公开审查，但由于这位记者拒绝与军方讨论他的电报，因此在他这种情况下无法存在公开审查。这一决定不适用于其他记者。

THE CHINA PRESS, 19 JAN 1938

Censorship
Dispute May
Bring Protest

Timperley Places Case
In Hands Of British
Consul-General

Mr. H. J. Timperley, correspondent for the Manchester Guardian, yesterday again placed his case in connection with the Japanese censorship of his news dispatch in the hands of the British Consul-General, Mr. Herbert Phillips, after he had failed to obtain a satisfactory settlement during his conversations with the Japanese Embassy spokesman, Mr. K. Okamura.

The affair, which arose from what Mr. Timperley describes as "suppression" of his cable message, is likely to lead to an official representation by the British Consul-General to Mr. S. Okamoto, Japanese Consul-General, although definite decision on the steps to be taken was still pending last night.

"Diplomatic Case"

Mr. Phillips told THE CHINA PRESS yesterday evening that the dispute centering on the censorship of the Guardian correspondent's message is now a "diplomatic case." A copy of his dispatch to the Guardian over which the censorship dispute arose, was yesterday given to the British official by the correspondent.

During his conversation with the Japanese spokesman, Mr. Timperley asked for an assurance that his cable messages to the Guardian will not be censored in the future. This assurance, however, the Japanese official was not prepared to give, stating that the Japanese army has the right to censor dispatches by virtue of its military occupation.

Failing to obtain the assurance, Mr. Timperley decided to place the case in the hands of the British Consul-General who had previously advised the correspondent to personally conduct preliminary negotiations with the Nipponese official.

May Become Test Case

Mr. Timperley stated last night that the issue brought up in the censorship of his cable message constitutes a test case on whether or not the Japanese authorities here have the right to institute a censorship of dispatches filed by British correspondents and incidentally of other foreign newspapermen.

In a letter to THE CHINA PRESS yesterday, Mr. Timperley pointed out that his message was not merely delayed, but was, in fact, suppressed. The message, he explained, has not been released so far for transmission.

争议可能

田伯烈将案件
移交英国
总领事

《曼彻斯特卫报》记者H. J. 田伯烈（H. J. Timperley）先生在与日本大使馆发言人冈村（K. Okamura）先生的会谈中未能获得令人满意的解决后，昨日再次将其关于日本审查其新闻电报的案件移交英国总领事赫伯特·菲利普斯（Herbert Phillips）先生处理。

此事起因于田伯烈先生所称的对其电缆消息的“压制”，这很可能导致英国总领事向日本总领事冈本（S. Okamoto）先生提出正式交涉，尽管截至昨晚，对于将采取何种步骤尚未作出明确决定。

“外交案件”

菲利普斯先生昨晚告诉《字林西报》，围绕《卫报》记者消息审查问题的争端现在是一个“外交案件”。引起审查争议的发给《卫报》的电报副本，昨日已由该记者交给这位英国官员。

在与日本发言人的谈话中，田伯烈先生要求保证他发给《卫报》的电缆消息将来不会受到审查。然而，日本官员不愿给予这一保证，声称日本军队凭借其军事占领有权审查电报。

由于未能获得保证，田伯烈先生决定将此案移交给英国总领事，后者此前曾建议该记者亲自与日本官员进行初步谈判。

可能成为判例

田伯烈先生昨晚表示，其电缆消息审查中提出的问题构成了一个判例，用以检验日本当局是否有权对英国记者以及其他外国新闻记者提交的电报实施审查。

在昨日致《字林西报》的一封信中，田伯烈先生指出，他的消息不仅仅是被延误，而是事实上被压制了。他解释说，该消息至今未被放行传输。

“(3) 日本当局在就此事与我联系之前等待了14个小时，然后要求我前往日本军事总部，这种行为已足够专横，但这并不构成我投诉的主要理由。我主张，日本无权以任何方式干涉英国记者为向国外传输而在电报局提交的任何消息。”
如果他们认为有理由对记者提出投诉，他们正确的行动方针肯定是向英国当局提出此事。如果允许日本压制他们不喜欢的电报，那么英国以及所有其他作为公共租界管理伙伴的列强为何不能主张同等的权利？
切勿忘记，尽管表面现象相反，日本并未正式向中国宣战。我们还要允许她既得利益又占便宜多久？”
**排队待发的消息**
田伯烈先生提交给电报局的相关消息内容如下：
“自数日前返回上海以来，调查了日军在南京及其他地方犯下的据报道的暴行 停 来自可靠目击者的口头叙述以及来自信誉无可置疑的个人信件提供了令人信服的证据，证明日军的行为及持续行为让人想起阿提拉及其匈人部落 停 一位有能力的外国观察员的调查显示，在长江三角洲，不少于三十万中国平民被屠杀，许多情况下是冷血屠杀 停 包括对幼儿在内的抢劫以及对平民丧心病狂的暴行，在敌对行动实际停止数周的地区仍继续有报道 停 此处较优秀的日本平民对日军在其他地方的可谴责行为深感羞耻，而上海本地发生的一系列日本士兵发狂事件加剧了这种羞耻感 停 今日《华北每日新闻》报道了一起特别令人厌恶的案件，一名醉酒的日本士兵因无法得到妇女和酒，开枪射杀了三名六十岁以上的中国妇女，并打伤了其他几名无辜平民 田伯烈。”

THE CHINA PRESS 18 JAN 1938

**Timperley Message To Guardian Causes Censorship Dispute**

Japanese Censors Decline To Transmit Report, Inform Correspondent 15 Hours After Cable Filed; British Embassy Told Of Case

SQUABBLE GIVEN FIRST AIRING AT NIPPON PRESS CONFERENCE; SETTLEMENT PENDING

The much-discussed question of Japanese censorship on cable messages became a matter of official discussion yesterday between local Japanese and British diplomatic representatives following the case in which the dispatch filed by Mr. H. J. Timperley, correspondent of the Manchester Guardian, was held up by the Nipponese censors.

Mr. Timperley's message, in which he reported that some 300,000 Chinese civilians had been slaughtered, many of them in cold blood, in the Yangtze delta war areas, was filed at 8 p.m. Sunday. At 10.45 o'clock yesterday morning—some 15 hours after his dispatch was filed—he was informed by Japanese censors that his message had failed to go through.

At the same time, Mr. Timperley was summoned by a member of the censorship office to visit the Nipponese military headquarters. It was suggested that an escort might be furnished to the correspondent to accompany him on the trip.

The British correspondent promptly rejected the request. He wanted to know, as he is a British subject, what right the censors had to hold up his message.

Report To British Embassy

Following the telephone conversation with the Japanese, Mr. Timperley reported the matter to the British Embassy, where he was referred to the British Consul-General, Mr. Herbert Phillips.

The British official subsequently brought the matter to the attention of Mr. S. Okamoto. A discussion took place and it was tentatively agreed that opinion on the case should be exchanged between Mr. Timperley and Mr. K. Okamura, Japanese Embassy spokesman, to find out whether a settlement on the matter could be made.

Mr. Timperley is scheduled to see Mr. Okamura this morning to discuss the question.

At the Japanese press conference yesterday evening, the spokesman stated that although cable censorship is a civilian service of the Japanese Government, the final decision in censoring press dispatches dealing with political and military questions rests with the embassy and military authorities respectively.

Delayed 15 Hours

It was brought up at the conference that, despite Japanese promises that journalists would immediately be notified whenever their cables were either censored or held, the dispatch of the Guardian correspondent was delayed for nearly 15 hours before the journalist was informed of the matter.

To this the spokesman made no reply, stating that an answer would be made after an inquiry is made into the matter.

One correspondent asked why, if censorship was a civilian service, was Mr. Timperley summoned to the Japanese military headquarters.

Answering the question, Mr. Okamura, the Embassy spokesman, said that although the censorship office was manned by civilian members of the Japanese Government, the Japanese army in occupation exercised the prerogative.

The report that the British correspondent was summoned to the military headquarters was not correct, he stated. Mr. Timperley, the spokesman explained, was only asked to accompany an official of the censorship organ to the office of the Japanese Military Attache, where the reason for the delay would be explained.

Asked whether this meant that the final decision rested with the military, the spokesman replied in the affirmative.

Regrets Over Error

Mr. Timperley, who was present at the conference, denied any mention at all was made of the Japanese Military Attache's office. He was asked to visit the Military Headquarters, he emphasized. Mr. Okamura then expressed his regret about the error, stating that the official had used the wrong term and that what he actually meant was the Military Attache's office.

The Guardian writer then asked whether or not his message was finally sent. He was told that it would be dispatched after certain points of it had been agreed upon between himself and the Japanese military. He was further informed that the military authorities could not get in touch with him, to which he answered that he was at home from 10 to 12.30 o'clock Sunday night.

"If it isn't sent," Mr. Timperley said, "what is to be done with it?"

"The Embassy spokesman will discuss the matter with you later."

"But I am not in a position to discuss the matter, as I have already reported it to the British authorities who will deal with the matter as they see fit." Furthermore, as the dispatch has been thus long delayed, there is no use of sending it at all now."

He was informed that Mr. Phillips had already spoken to Mr. Okamura regarding the matter. Mr. Timperley then left the conference.

〔此处转录不清〕

The Japanese authorities, the spokesman reiterated, were enforcing censorship by virtue of their taking over of Chinese Governmental organs in Shanghai following the evacuation of the city.

"It has no relation to the question of whether or not the cables run through Japanese-occupied territory," the official stated.

While censorship was being enforced by a civilian personnel, final decision as to whether or not dispatches were considered objectionable rested with the military authorities in the matter involved related to military questions.

"Should diplomatic questions be involved, the Japanese Embassy would be the last authority to decide," the spokesman stated."

《字林西报》 1938年1月18日

**田伯烈发给《卫报》的消息引发审查争议**

日本审查员拒绝转发报告，在电报提交15小时后通知记者；英国大使馆获悉此案

争吵首次在日本新闻发布会上公开；解决方案待定

备受关注的日本对电缆消息审查问题，在《曼彻斯特卫报》记者H. J. 田伯烈先生提交的电报被日本审查员扣留一案发生后，于昨日成为当地日本和英国外交代表之间官方讨论的事项。

田伯烈先生的消息报道了在长江三角洲战区，约30万中国平民被屠杀，其中许多人是被冷血杀害的，该消息于周日晚8点提交。昨天上午10点45分——即在他提交电报约15小时后——他接到日本审查员的通知，称他的消息未能发出。

与此同时，田伯烈先生被审查办公室的一名成员召见，要求前往日本军事总部。有人建议可以为该记者提供护送人员陪同前往。

这位英国记者立即拒绝了这一要求。他想知道，作为一名英国臣民，审查员有何权利扣留他的消息。

向英国大使馆报告

在与日本人进行电话交谈后，田伯烈先生向英国大使馆报告了此事，随后被引荐给英国总领事赫伯特·菲利普斯先生。

这位英国官员随后将此事提请日本总领事冈本（S. Okamoto）先生注意。双方进行了讨论，并初步同意由田伯烈先生与日本大使馆发言人冈村（K. Okamura）先生交换意见，以查明此事能否达成和解。

田伯烈先生定于今天上午会见冈村先生讨论此问题。

在昨晚的日本新闻发布会上，发言人表示，虽然电缆审查是日本政府的一项民事服务，但对涉及政治和军事问题的新闻电报进行审查的最终决定权分别属于大使馆和军事当局。

延误15小时

会议上有人提出，尽管日本承诺一旦记者的电报被审查或扣留会立即通知记者，但《卫报》记者的电报在记者获知此事前被延误了近15小时。

对此，发言人未作答复，称将在对此事进行调查后作出回答。

一名记者问道，如果审查是一项民事服务，为何田伯烈先生被召往日本军事总部。

回答这个问题时，大使馆发言人冈村先生说，虽然审查办公室由日本政府的文职人员组成，但占领军行使了这一特权。

他表示，有关英国记者被召往军事总部的报道是不正确的。发言人解释说，田伯烈先生只是被要求陪同审查机构的一名官员前往日本武官办公室，那里将对延误原因作出解释。

当被问及这是否意味着最终决定权在军方时，发言人给予了肯定答复。

对错误表示遗憾

出席会议的田伯烈先生否认有人提及日本武官办公室。他强调，他被要求前往的是军事总部。冈村先生随后对这一错误表示遗憾，称该官员用词不当，他实际指的是武官办公室。

这位《卫报》撰稿人随后询问他的消息最终是否已发出。他被告知，在他与日本军方就其中的某些要点达成一致后，消息将会发出。他还被告知，军事当局无法与他取得联系，对此他回答说，他在周日晚10点至12点半期间在家。

“如果还没发出去，”田伯烈先生说，“那该怎么处理？”

“大使馆发言人稍后将与您讨论此事。”

“但我无法讨论此事，因为我已向英国当局报告，他们将酌情处理此事。”此外，由于电报已被如此长时间延误，现在发送也已毫无用处。”

他获悉菲利普斯先生已就此事与冈村先生进行过交谈。田伯烈先生随后离开了发布会。

〔此处转录不清〕

发言人重申，日本当局凭借其在撤离城市后接管上海中国政府机关的权力，正在实施审查。

“这与电缆是否通过日本占领区的问题无关，”该官员表示。

虽然审查由文职人员执行，但在涉及军事问题的事项中，电报是否被视为不妥的最终决定权在于军事当局。

“如果涉及外交问题，日本大使馆将是最后的裁决机构，”发言人表示。”

田伯烈先生被要求

军方办公室

发言人作出解释

昨日，外国记者向其报社发送的电讯受审查一事再次成为焦点。当时，《曼彻斯特卫报》记者 H. J. 田伯烈（H. J. Timperley）先生于上午获悉，他于周日晚间发出的电讯未通过审查。他被要求随同审查员前往虹口日本武官办公室，但他拒绝了这一要求，并就此事与英国大使馆进行了联系。

在昨日下午的日本新闻发布会上，就审查制度问题进行了长时间讨论后，使馆发言人表示，除非在上海的外国记者同意与负责的日本官员讨论删除后者认为不当的部分电讯内容，否则无法实施“公开审查制度”。

该发言人补充说，这位英国记者受邀前往武官办公室，“是为了从一位负责的日本军官那里获得解释，说明其电讯中哪些部分被认为是不当的”。审查员提出陪同田伯烈先生前往。

发言人对审查员在邀请田伯烈先生时使用“军事总部”一词表示遗憾。发言人称：“这可能引起了误解。”

发言人重申，日本当局之所以实施审查，是因为在包围上海之后，他们接管了上海的中国政府机构。

该官员表示：“这与电报是否经过日军占领区的问题无关。”

虽然审查工作由文职人员执行，但如果所涉事项与军事问题有关，则关于电讯是否被视为不当的最终决定权在于军事当局。

发言人表示，如果涉及外交问题，则由日本大使馆作为裁决机构。

THE CHINA PRESS

GuardianC orrespondent
Finds China’s Leaders
Unshaken In Confidence

H. J. Timperley Reports Observations
On Hankow Political Tempo;
Chiang Interviewed

Grimly determined to fight to the bitter end in defense of China’s political integrity, the majority of high National Government officials in Hankow, led by Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, appeared to be confident that the nation would eventually come out on top in the present struggle, Mr. H. J. Timperley, correspondent of the Manchester Guardian, found after close observation of the Chinese political tempo during his recent trip to the Wuhan city.
Mr. Timperley, who had a two-hour talk with the Generalissimo, found the latter in splendid health and spirits, the correspondent revealed yesterday in an interview with THE CHINA PRESS.

**Peace Talks**
Questioned on the current report of peace talks in Hankow, Mr. Timperley stated:
“So far as I could find out, there is no such thing as a peace-at-any-price group in Hankow. Probably there are certain people in the Government who would be prepared to make more concessions than others; but even those who belong in this category seemed to feel that there was no alternative, but to carry on the struggle in view of the improbability that the Japanese would consider terms that would be at all acceptable.”
The fall of Nanking, Mr. Timperley thought, came as quite a shock to many of the Government officials. They were, however, rapidly adjusting themselves to the situation and were now grimly preparing to carry on what it is now recognized will necessarily be a long and bitter struggle, the correspondent reported.

**Chiang Interviewed**
During his long session with the Generalissimo, the latter expressed his conviction of China’s final victory to Mr. Timperley in the following words:
“Although we may have suffered defeats on the battlefield,” the Generalissimo told the correspondent, “that doesn’t mean that the war is over. Japan will find it easier to occupy territory than to maintain herself in the areas where her troops have gained a foothold.”
Continuing, the Generalissimo said: “Even if the Chinese army did nothing, the Japanese troops would still find it an expensive business to consolidate their position. If, on the other hand, we engage them with our mobile units they will find it a difficult matter to keep their communications open.

**Powers’ Obligations**
“While we will do our best with our limited resources, we hope that Britain and America and other friendly powers will realize that China is now fighting their battle as well as her own. While we do not necessarily expect that they should wage war on our behalf, we do ask that they should live up to their obligations as co-signatories of the League covenant and other international pacts and help us wherever possible,” the Generalissimo said in his interview with Mr. Timperley.

The Guardian correspondent went to Hankow in the middle of last month, traveling by air from Hong-Kong to the Wuhan city. On his return journey he was a passenger on the international train which reached the colony on Christmas Day. He reported that his observations showed that the Canton-Hankow railway has not been seriously damaged as a result of the repeated aerial attacks. The train, which was ahead of its schedule on one or two occasions, went through without any untoward incident.

**Hankow Crowded**
Hankow, as a result of the large influx of refugees and government officials, is extremely crowded. A new-comer is usually confronted with difficulty in finding bed if he has not made arrangements beforehand; the writer reported.
When Mr. Timperley arrived in Hankow, he saw many wounded Chinese soldiers, wearing blue coats with embroidered Red Cross insignia, walking along the Bund. Some of these men were being carried by their comrades.
The correspondent heard high praise for the work being performed by the Hankow International Red Cross, which is headed by the Mayor of Hankow, with Mr. G. S. Moss, the British Consul-General as the Vice-Chairman.
Extensive relief and medical work of the organization is being efficiently carried out under the direction of Dr. J. W. Maxwell, veteran medical missionary, who is well-known in Shanghai for his work with the Henry Lester Institute of Medical Research. Dr. Maxwell is now the executive secretary of the Hankow International Red Cross.

**Gives Cash Grant**
Generalissimo Chiang during his conversation with Mr. Timperley was much interested in hearing of conditions in Shanghai. He readily approved the request made by the correspondent, who is a member of the Publicity and Appeals Committee of the Shanghai International Red Cross, for replacing with a new cash grant a portion of the Liberty Bonds given to the Red Cross as a part of the Government’s $1,000,000 donation.
“It is gratifying to learn since my return to Shanghai,” Mr. Timperley said yesterday, “that a sum of $300,000 cash has already been received by the Red Cross from Hankow. A large part of the money has already been applied to relief purposes.”

《字林西报》

卫报记者发现
中国领导人
信心未动摇

H. J. 田伯烈报道对汉口政治节奏的观察；
采访蒋介石

《曼彻斯特卫报》记者 H. J. 田伯烈先生在最近前往武汉期间，密切观察了中国政治动态，他发现，以蒋介石委员长为首的汉口国民政府大多数高级官员决心坚决战斗到底，以捍卫中国的政治完整，并似乎有信心国家将在目前的斗争中最终获胜。
田伯烈先生曾与委员长进行了两小时的谈话，他发现委员长身心健康、精神饱满，该记者昨日在接受《字林西报》采访时透露了这一情况。

**和谈**
当被问及目前关于汉口和谈的报道时，田伯烈先生表示：
“据我了解，汉口中并不存在所谓‘不惜任何代价求和’的派系。可能政府中有些人愿意比其他人做出更多让步；但即使是属于这一类的人似乎也感到，鉴于日本不太可能考虑任何可以接受的条款，除了继续斗争外别无选择。”
田伯烈先生认为，南京的陷落令许多政府官员感到相当震惊。然而，他们正在迅速适应局势，并现在严阵以待，准备进行一场现在公认必然是长期而艰苦的斗争，该记者报道说。

**采访蒋介石**
在与委员长的长时间会谈中，后者向田伯烈先生表达了他对中国最终胜利的信念，原话如下：
“虽然我们在战场上可能遭受了失败，”委员长告诉记者，“但这并不意味着战争已经结束。日本会发现，占领领土比在其部队已站稳脚跟的地区维持自身存在更容易。”
委员长接着说：“即使中国军队什么都不做，日军仍会发现巩固其阵地是一项代价高昂的工作。另一方面，如果我们用机动部队与他们交战，他们会发现保持通讯畅通是一件困难的事。

**列强的义务**
“虽然我们将利用有限的资源尽力而为，但我们希望英国、美国和其他友好国家认识到，中国现在不仅是在为自己的战斗，也是在为他们的战斗。虽然我们不一定期望他们代表我们发动战争，但我们确实要求他们履行作为《国际联盟盟约》及其他国际公约共同签署国的义务，并在可能的情况下帮助我们，”委员长在接受田伯烈先生采访时说。

这位《卫报》记者于上月月中旬前往汉口，从香港乘飞机抵达武汉。在返程途中，他乘坐国际列车，于圣诞节当天抵达殖民地（香港）。他报告说，他的观察表明，粤汉铁路并未因 repeated 空袭而受到严重破坏。这列火车在一两次甚至提前到达，全程未发生任何意外事件。

**汉口拥挤**
由于大量难民和政府官员涌入，汉口极其拥挤。作者报道说，新来者如果没有事先安排，通常在寻找床位时会遇到困难。
当田伯烈先生抵达汉口时，他看到许多受伤的中国士兵，身穿绣有红十字标志的蓝外套，沿着外滩行走。其中一些人正由战友抬着。
该记者听到人们对汉口国际红十字会的工作给予高度赞扬，该会由汉口市长领导，英国总领事 G. S. 莫斯（G. S. Moss）先生担任副主席。
该组织广泛的救济和医疗工作正在资深医学传教士 J. W. 麦克斯韦（J. W. Maxwell）博士的指导下有效开展，他因在上海亨利·雷士德医学研究所的工作而闻名。麦克斯韦博士现任汉口国际红十字会执行秘书。

**提供现金拨款**
蒋介石委员长在与田伯烈先生交谈时，对了解上海的情况非常感兴趣。他欣然批准了该记者的请求。田伯烈是上海国际红十字会宣传与募捐委员会成员，他请求用新的现金拨款替换作为政府100万美元捐款一部分提供给红十字会的部分自由债券。
“令我欣慰的是，自从我回到上海后，”田伯烈先生昨天说，“红十字会已经收到了来自汉口的30万美元现金。这笔钱的大部分已经用于救济目的。”

Invite Journalist

Timperley, Manchester
Guardian Writer,
Refuses Bid

ATROCITY STORIES
BRING INVITATION

Interfering With Cable
Messages Protested
To Embassy

Mr. H. J. Timperley, correspondent for the Manchester Guardian at 10:45 o'clock this morning refused an invitation extended by the Japanese censorship office to pay a visit to the Nipponese military headquarters in Hongkew. At the same time he was informed that a despatch sent to the cable office shortly before 4 o'clock last night which summed up Japanese atrocities committed in various areas on Chinese civilians during the past month or so had been held up.

The British correspondent not only rejected the invitation to discuss the matter with the Japanese military, but also demanded to know what right the censors had to hold up a message sent by a British subject. Following his brief conversation with the censors by telephone, Mr. Timperley informed the British Embassy which is now investigating the matter.

It is understood that after carefully checking information at hand, Mr. Timperley came to the conclusion that some 300,000 Chinese civilians had been executed by the Japanese military following their occupation of the Shanghai-Nanking area. These findings, as well as data on looting and raping, made up the message which the Nipponese censors felt violated the rule that information likely to harm the military must not be despatched.

Mr. Timperley is to call at the British Embassy office at 3 o'clock this afternoon to discuss the matter. It is understood that the censorship office kindly offered to supply an escort for the correspondent on his trip to Hongkew. The British journalist is believed to be the first newspaperman invited to have a heart to heart talk with the Nipponese military about a cable message.

Some time ago a Japanese press spokesman assured correspondents that when censorship was necessary, every effort would be made to inform the correspondent affected within three hours of the time the cable was filed. Mr. Timperley received his notification approximately 15 hours after the objectionable message was in the hands of the censors.

今天上午10点45分，《曼彻斯特卫报》记者 H. J. 田伯烈先生拒绝了日本审查办公室发出的前往虹口日本军事总部参观的邀请。同时他被告知，昨晚接近4点发往电报局的一份总结了过去一个月左右日军在中国各地平民犯下暴行的电讯被扣留。

这位英国记者不仅拒绝了与日本军方讨论此事的邀请，还要求知道审查员有何权利扣留一名英国臣民发送的消息。在与审查员通过电话进行简短交谈后，田伯烈先生通知了正在调查此事的英国大使馆。

据悉，在仔细核实手头信息后，田伯烈先生得出结论，约有30万中国平民在日军占领沪宁地区后被处决。这些发现以及关于抢劫和强奸的数据构成了该消息的内容，日本审查员认为这违反了不得发送可能损害军方利益的信息的规定。

田伯烈先生将于今天下午3点前往英国大使馆办公室讨论此事。据悉，审查办公室好意提出为该记者前往虹口的行程提供护卫。这位英国记者被认为是第一位受邀就电报消息与日本军方进行坦诚交谈的新闻工作者。

不久前，一位日本新闻发言人向记者保证，在有必要进行审查时，将尽一切努力在电报提交后三小时内通知受影响记者。田伯烈先生在收到该不当消息约15小时后才收到通知，当时该消息已在审查员手中。

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Monday, April 26, 1937.

Timperley Moving
Office To Nanking
Mr. H. J. Timperley, correspondent for the Manchester Guardian and advisory editor of Asia magazine, has decided to transfer his headquarters to Nanking and from May 1 he will be located at the Metropolitan hotel there. Since he came from Peiping some months ago he has been establishing contacts and gaining first-hand knowledge of Shanghai problems but he has now concluded that the capital is his logical permanent base.

In addition to the connections mentioned, Mr. Timperley will write Nanking correspondence for the Christian Science Monitor and other papers and periodicals, and it is his intention to begin work at once on a book. During the intervals of active newspaper work he has been engaged for two years in making a study of the historical basis of the Sino-Japanese conflict and he will now begin to digest the material collected.
Mr. Timperley will be the first and for the time being the only British correspondent to be regularly established at Nanking.

Factory Boys
Enter Winter
School Here

Social Experiment Being
Conducted Under Lead
Of Timperley

HARMONICA CLASS
PROVES POPULAR

Co-operation Is Given
By Chinese
Y.M.C.A.

An unusually interesting experi-
ment in social work is being carried
out in the Yangtsepoo district for
the benefit of Chinese boys employ-
ed in factories of the Kinchow Road
area. This is an outgrowth of a
summer physical school established
last June under the direction of Mr.
H. J. Timperley, Manchester Guar-
dian Correspondent, and other resi-
dents of Shanghai. The original
scheme proved to be so successful
that it was decided to make it per-
manent and this has been done with
the co-operation of the Chinese
Y.M.C.A. here.
A representative of THE CHINA
PRESS has visited the physical
school to learn something of the
winter program which is now under
way and becoming increasingly
popular with a growing number of
boys. Recreation periods are being
held in the evening at the Kinchow
Road Primary School through the
courtesy of the Shanghai Municipal
Council, and these are conducted
under the expert direction of Mr.
F. T. Chen of the Y.M.C.A.

Start Harmonica Class

Mr. Timperley pays frequent
visits to the school and takes a
personal interest in its development
from week to week. One of the
most gratifying improvements
which has been made is the in-
auguration of a harmonica class for
the boys. This has proven success-
ful in that it involves a small
initial outlay in equipment and
appeals to boys of all ages. Many
of the boys spend a large part of
their very limited leisure time in
harmonica practice and have be-
come quite expert with these simple
instruments.
The winter physical school is the
outgrowth of a plan instituted here
last May by a committee which in-
cluded in its membership Mr. Tim-
perley as Chairman, Baroness
Leonie Ungern-Sternberg, Madame
Paul Premet, Dr. Agnes Roman,
Mr. John S. Barr and Mr. Franklin
Fu.
Boys attending the classes are
drawn mainly from the small shops
and factories in the district at which
they receive little or nothing for
their efforts put in during a work-
ing day lasting from 10 to 12 hours.
Before the inauguration of the
school they were without any real
facilities for recreation and found
it difficult to find ways and means
to leave the places of their employ-
ment even for brief periods of time.

Enjoy School

Like the summer school, the
winter school is proving to be com-
paratively simple and easy to
operate, while the boys themselves
are appreciative and easy to handle.
They take great delight in all
aspects of the work and even seem
to enjoy the routine exercises in
which they are drilled.
Although the classes have been
conducted out of doors up until a
few weeks ago, a large hall in the
school is available for use during
inclement weather. Those in charge
now feel that the winter classes
when viewed from the standpoint
of the small expense involved show
encouraging results. It is now hoped
that the idea will spread in the
Yangtsepoo district and elsewhere
in Shanghai where there is a crying
need for such provision for young
workers.

工厂童工
在此进入
冬季学校

在田伯烈领导下
进行的社会实验

口琴班
深受欢迎

得到中国
青年会
的合作

一项不同寻常且有趣的社会工作实验正在杨树浦地区开展，旨在造福锦州路区域工厂雇佣的中国男童。这是去年六月在《曼彻斯特卫报》记者H. J. 田伯烈先生和其他上海居民指导下建立的夏季体育学校的延伸成果。最初的计划证明非常成功，因此决定将其永久化，这一工作是在此地中国青年会的合作下完成的。
《字林西报》的一名代表参观了这所体育学校，以了解目前正在进行的冬季项目的一些情况，该项目在日益增多的男童中越来越受欢迎。娱乐活动时间安排在晚上，地点设在锦州路小学，承蒙上海公共租界工部局的好意提供场地，这些活动在中国青年会的F. T. 陈先生的专业指导下进行。

开设口琴班

田伯烈先生经常访问学校，并对其每周的发展给予个人关注。最令人欣慰的改进之一是为学生开设了口琴班。事实证明这是成功的，因为它所需的初始设备投入很小，并且吸引了各个年龄段的男童。许多男童将他们非常有限的闲暇时间的很大一部分用于口琴练习，并且在使用这些简单乐器方面变得相当熟练。
冬季体育学校是去年五月由一个委员会发起的计划的延伸成果，该委员会成员包括主席田伯烈先生、莱奥妮·翁格恩-施特恩贝格女男爵（Baroness Leonie Ungern-Sternberg）、保罗·普雷梅特夫人（Madame Paul Premet）、阿格尼丝·罗曼博士（Dr. Agnes Roman）、约翰·S. 巴尔先生（Mr. John S. Barr）和富兰克林·傅先生（Mr. Franklin Fu）。
参加课程的男童主要来自该地区的小商店和工厂，他们在每天长达10到12小时的工作日中付出的努力几乎得不到任何报酬。在学校成立之前，他们没有任何真正的娱乐设施，发现很难找到方法和途径离开工作地点，哪怕是短暂的时间。

享受学校生活

与夏季学校一样，冬季学校也被证明操作相对简单容易，而男童们本身也很感激且易于管理。他们对工作的各个方面都感到非常高兴，甚至似乎很享受让他们接受的常规训练。
虽然直到几周前课程一直在户外进行，但学校内有一个大厅可在天气恶劣时使用。负责人现在认为，从涉及的少量费用来看，冬季课程取得了令人鼓舞的成果。现在希望这一理念能在杨树浦地区以及上海其他年轻工人迫切需要有此类设施的地区传播开来。

NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, FRIDAY, MAY 1, 1936

A TERRIBLE TOIL

By an undesigned coincidence, Mr. H. J. Timperley's eloquent plea for consideration of the plight of a section of young workers in Shanghai's rapidly expanding industrialism appeared yesterday with the publication of the findings of Dr. Bernard E. Read, Dr. S. G. Hatem, Mr. Ding Yu-bao and Mr. Lee Wei-yung on their investigation of the "Chromium Plating and Polishing Trade." Their report, No. 6 of the Special Report Series of the Chinese Medical Association, can be bought for fifty cents from the offices of the Association at 41 Tse pang Road, Shanghai. It should be obtained and studied by all who have at heart the interests of this great city and the slightest spark of humane solicitude for the welfare of their fellow-creatures. The scientific basis of the report gives exceptional authority to its revelations which may truly be described as Dickensian. They indicate that the grim horrors known to Victorian England are being reproduced in Shanghai, where in the last few years the sudden creation of small industrial enterprises operated in badly improvised buildings has given rise to conditions demanding immediate attention. Charles Kingsley, in writing his "Water Babies" had no more inspiring topic for his philanthropic pen than the excruciating agony of these wretched little slaves who have been drawn into the vortex of an unconsidered industrial system by the pressure of economic facts and public ignorance taken unawares. Mr. Timperley not unnaturally considers that the Shanghai Municipal Council has a special responsibility in the matter. His view will be strongly supported—indeed it has been anticipated in these columns for some time, since in 1934 this journal disclosed certain of the worst features of the silk industry, with its attendant evils of labour-recruitment, and the insanitary and dangerous conditions of the li houses. Moreover, a few weeks ago in discussing the occupational census figures, it was pointed out that the character of the population of the Settlement had radically changed in that the prominence of industrial workers had brought to the fore serious economic problems of which the Council was bound to take increasingly emphatic note.

The revelations now made show that the Council is not indifferent, for Dr. Read and his able co-adjutors could not have obtained their information without the wholehearted co-operation of the Settlement authorities to which their report pays tribute. Yet that document has an important effect on the Council's position, in that, beyond the peradventure of a doubt, it will be taken as the basis of public support for a definite acceptance of the Council's responsibility for the fullest investigation of labour conditions in the area within its control. The Report is not, of course, purely an indictment. It has the important object of giving a scientific appreciation of the conditions of the industry so that employers may intelligently modify their methods for the purpose of getting the best possible results from their enterprise. The employers are not necessarily callous or inhumane. Their own economic condition is by no means expansive and their acceptance of the terrible sacrifices of young life is due more to thoughtlessness and ignorance than to any deliberate cruelty. Yet the Council, as the representative body of the Settlement, has to consider means for the better education of employers, the better instruction of public opinion and, above all, the better provision of reasonable amenities for the employees. The communist peril may or may not be great. Nothing could contribute more surely to the manufacture of rebels against the social system, whether in the guise of communists or even worse, than the perpetuation of this vile exploitation of child labour. Reform cannot come in a lightning flash. The plain duty to prepare the ground for it and strengthen the appropriate administrative machinery, within the limits of their power, now devolves upon the authorities of the International Settlement. It becomes an elementary form of vindicating the Council's sense of civic responsibility.

The Read Report, in dealing with the chromium plating and polishing trade which employs over 1,200 workers, makes three important points:

The general health of the class from which the workers are recruited is below the average normal level, so that without any occupational hazards the workers are handicapped in keeping a decent standard of health.

The labour turnover is great. Workers injured or poisoned are usually discharged and their places filled. So clinical findings give a fallacious return of low incidence of disease. The average working-life of these workers is 3 years 4 months.

The immaturity of the young workers makes them more susceptible to the hazards of the industry and the poor conditions around them.

When it is realized that these workers are brought to Shanghai after purchase by middlemen from their parents and are, under the cover of an apprentice system which is merely a tragic euphemism for slavery, condemned to work themselves to the bone with totally inadequate nourishment and without the ordinary amenities of life, the gravity of the indictment which Mr. Timperley has preferred and which is so vividly supported by the scientists' report cannot be ignored. Dr. Read and his colleagues have rendered a great public service. It is now the duty of the community to see that it has not been rendered in vain—not merely on humanitarian grounds, but for the sake of the good name of Shanghai.

《字林西报》，1936年5月1日，星期五

可怕的苦役

出于一种非刻意的巧合，H. J. 廷珀利先生恳请人们关注上海迅速发展的工业主义中部分年轻工人困境的有力呼吁，于昨日与伯纳德·E·里德（Bernard E. Read）博士、S. G. 哈特姆（S. G. Hatem）博士、丁玉宝（音译）先生和李维庸（音译）先生关于“镀铬与抛光行业”调查结果的发布同时见报。他们的报告是中华医学会特别报告系列的第6号，可在上海泽邦路41号该会办事处以五十分的价格购得。凡关心这座大城市利益、对同胞福祉怀有丝毫人道关怀的人士，均应获取并研读此报告。该报告的科学基础使其披露的内容具有非凡的权威性，这些内容真可谓狄更斯式的写照。它们表明，维多利亚时代的英国所熟知的可怕恐怖景象正在上海重演；在过去几年里，在简陋凑合的建筑中突然涌现的小型工业企业，造成了亟需立即关注的状况。查尔斯·金斯利在撰写《水孩子》时，其充满慈善情怀的笔触所遇到的鼓舞人心的题材，莫过于这些可怜的小奴隶所遭受的极度痛苦；他们因经济现实的压力和公众的无知而被卷入一个未经深思熟虑的工业体系的漩涡之中。廷珀利先生认为上海公共租界工部局在此事上负有特殊责任，这并不奇怪。他的观点将得到有力支持——事实上，本报专栏此前已对此有所预期，因为早在1934年，本报就揭露了丝绸业的一些最恶劣特征，包括其伴随的招工弊病以及里弄房屋的不卫生和危险状况。此外，几周前在讨论职业人口普查数据时，曾指出租界人口的性质发生了根本性变化，即产业工人的突出地位使严重的经济问题凸显出来，工部局不得不日益重视这些问题。

目前的披露显示，工部局并非漠不关心，因为若无租界当局的全心合作，里德博士及其能干的助手们便无法获得这些信息，他们的报告对此表示了敬意。然而，该文件对工部局的立场具有重要影响，因为它毫无疑问将被视为公众支持的基础，促使工部局明确承担对其管辖区域内劳动状况进行全面调查的责任。当然，该报告并非纯粹的控诉。它有一个重要目标，即对该行业的状况进行科学评估，以便雇主能够明智地调整其方法，从而从其企业中获得尽可能好的结果。雇主们未必冷酷无情或不人道。他们自身的经济状况绝非宽裕，他们接受年轻生命的可怕牺牲，更多是由于疏忽和无知，而非蓄意残忍。然而，工部局作为租界的代表机构，必须考虑如何更好地教育雇主、更好地引导舆论，尤其是为员工提供更合理的便利设施。共产主义威胁或许大，或许不大。没有什么比延续这种对童工的卑鄙剥削更能确保制造出反对社会制度的反叛者，无论其伪装成共产主义者还是更糟的角色。改革不可能一蹴而就。在国际租界当局权力范围内，为改革奠定基础并加强相应行政机制的明确职责，现在落到了他们肩上。这成为证明工部局具备市政责任感的一种基本形式。

里德报告在处理雇佣超过1,200名工人的镀铬和抛光行业时，提出了三个重要观点：

招募工人的阶层整体健康状况低于正常平均水平，因此即使没有任何职业危害，工人在维持体面的健康标准方面也处于不利地位。

人员流动率很高。受伤或中毒的工人通常被解雇，并由他人填补空缺。因此，临床发现给出了发病率低的虚假回报。这些工人的平均工作年限为3年4个月。

年轻工人的不成熟使他们更容易受到行业危害及周围恶劣条件的影响。

当人们意识到这些工人是被中间商从父母手中买断后带到上海的，并且在仅仅是奴隶制的悲剧委婉说法的学徒制度掩护下，注定要在营养严重不足且缺乏日常生活基本便利的条件下拼命工作直至骨瘦如柴时，廷珀利先生提出的指控以及科学家报告所生动支持的指控，其严重性不容忽视。里德博士及其同事为公众做出了巨大贡献。现在社区有责任确保这一贡献没有白费——这不仅出于人道主义理由，也是为了维护上海的良好声誉。
